beginner: Collards like rich, loose soil that holds moisture but still drains well. Mix in plenty of compost before planting, since these big leafy plants are hungry feeders. They grow in most garden soils, but do best when the soil is fertile and never bone dry or waterlogged.
seasoned: Collards are not fussy about soil texture and grow across a wide range, but they perform best in a fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam high in organic matter. Because they are leafy heavy feeders held in the ground for months, work in plenty of compost before planting and keep moisture even. Tough, stringy leaves and stalled growth follow soil that either ponds water or bakes dry, so steady drainage and steady moisture both matter.

beginner: Collards grow best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, around 6.0 to 6.8. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. If you have had clubroot, keeping the soil closer to neutral helps hold it back.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 6.8; collards still grow across a wider 5.5 to 7.5 band. Holding the soil toward neutral, roughly 6.8 to 7.2, also helps suppress clubroot, a key brassica soil disease, so a grower with clubroot history should lean to the high end.

beginner: Collards grow a lot of leaves, so they need regular feeding to stay deep green and tender. Mix some fertilizer into the soil when you plant, feed again about 3 to 4 weeks later, and give a light feed after a big harvest so it grows fresh leaves. Do not overdo it, since too much fertilizer makes soft growth that bugs love.
seasoned: Collards are leafy and N-hungry, and steady nitrogen drives the deep green color and tender growth that make the crop. Work a balanced fertilizer into the bed at planting, then side-dress with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks later, and feed again after a heavy cutting to push new leaves. Extension guides commonly cite a nitrogen side-dressing such as calcium nitrate or 27-3-3 along the row; on long-held plants a feed every 3 to 4 weeks keeps them productive. Avoid overdoing nitrogen, which softens growth and draws aphids.

beginner: Time to feed your collards.
seasoned: Time to side-dress your collards with nitrogen.

beginner: Use a balanced vegetable fertilizer at planting, then a nitrogen-rich feed like blood meal as the plant grows.
seasoned: A balanced feed such as 10-10-10 at planting, then nitrogen side-dressings (calcium nitrate, blood meal, or 27-3-3) 3 to 4 weeks later and after heavy cutting to keep tender leaves coming.

beginner: Follow the label rate for a balanced fertilizer at planting and a nitrogen-rich feed as it grows.
seasoned: About 1.5 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 feet of row at planting, then side-dress roughly half a cup of calcium nitrate (or the label rate of a nitrogen source) per 25 feet of row every 3 to 4 weeks on long-held plants.

beginner: Collards do well next to aromatic herbs, onions, and quick cool-season crops like lettuce and beets. The main thing is to keep them away from other cabbage-family plants, which share their pests and diseases, so planting them together makes problems worse.
seasoned: Most collard companion pairings are traditional rather than research-tested. The ones worth acting on are practical: aromatic herbs and alliums as scent-based deterrents against the cabbage-family pests that hammer collards in the South, and quick cool-season crops like lettuce and beets as interplants that use space while the collards are small. The well-grounded caution is to separate collards from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cole-crop pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect.

beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for collards; their strong smell is said to help confuse and deter cabbage pests.
seasoned: Onions are one of the better-supported brassica companions. Their pungent allium scent helps mask the collards from cabbage-family pests, loopers, cabbageworms, and root maggots, that hunt partly by smell, and extension trial work including onion in a mix with cole crops showed reduced caterpillar damage. Alliums are shallow-rooted and undemanding, so they tuck around collards without competing for much.

beginner: Dill is a classic friend for cabbage-family plants. Its strong smell is said to put off pests, and its flowers bring in helpful insects.
seasoned: Dill works for collards mainly through beneficial insects. Its umbel flowers attract parasitoid wasps and predators like hoverflies and ladybugs that prey on the aphids and cabbage caterpillars collards draw, and extension work pairing aromatic umbels with brassicas has shown reduced caterpillar damage. Let some dill flower for the benefit, and site it nearby rather than crowding the collards.

beginner: Lettuce grows fast and low, so you can tuck it between young collard plants to use the space while the collards fill in.
seasoned: Lettuce and collards interplant well on structure and timing rather than chemistry. Lettuce is shallow-rooted and quick, collards taller and slower, so the lettuce uses the open ground and light between young collard plants and is harvested before the collards spread. Expect an efficient use of the bed in the cool shoulder season, not pest protection.

beginner: Keep collards away from other cabbage-family plants like broccoli, cabbage, kale, and cauliflower. They share the same pests and diseases, so planting them together makes problems worse.
seasoned: Planting collards cheek-by-jowl with their brassica relatives, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, kale, Brussels sprouts, concentrates the whole family's shared pests (cabbage worms, loopers, flea beetles, harlequin bugs, root maggots) and shared diseases in one spot, and repeated same-family planting lets soil-borne clubroot build up. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow each year.

beginner: You'll see ragged holes eaten in the big leaves, green caterpillars on the plant, and little dark droppings. Some caterpillars loop up in the middle as they crawl.
seasoned: Ragged holes chewed through the leaves, with green caterpillars and dark frass on the foliage. Imported cabbageworms are velvety green; cabbage loopers move in a looping arch; diamondback larvae are small and wriggle when disturbed. Because collards are sold and eaten as whole leaves, even modest feeding scars the crop.

beginner: These are caterpillars that hatch from eggs laid by white butterflies and small moths. They love cabbage-family plants like collards and chew the leaves, which are the part you eat.
seasoned: The larvae of the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth feed on brassica foliage; the adults are white or brownish butterflies and moths that lay eggs on the leaves. Caterpillar pressure runs especially long on collards in the warm South, where the crop is in the ground most of the year.

beginner: Spray a product called Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or pick the caterpillars and eggs off by hand from under the leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
seasoned: Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) or spinosad, which target caterpillars, and hand-pick larvae and eggs from leaf undersides. Repeat after rain, since Bt breaks down.

beginner: Cover plants with a light fabric row cover right after planting to keep the butterflies and moths from laying eggs. Clear away old cabbage-family plants, and watch for the first white butterflies as your signal to act.
seasoned: Use floating row cover from transplanting to exclude the egg-laying adults, clean up brassica debris that shelters pupae, and scout for the first white butterflies as a spray cue.

beginner: Shield-shaped black-and-orange (or black-and-red) bugs on the leaves, which develop white or yellow spots, then brown and look tattered. It is mostly a warm-region problem and loves collards.
seasoned: Shield-shaped bugs up to about 3/8 inch, brightly black-and-yellow or black-and-red, feeding with piercing-sucking mouthparts that leave white stipples; affected leaves brown and look tattered, and heavy feeding wilts and deforms plants. A warm-region pest that prefers collards, mustard, and kale over other cole crops, and a leading reason summer collards in the Deep South get buggy.

beginner: The harlequin bug is a colorful stink-bug relative that pierces the leaves and sucks the juices, leaving pale blotches. It strongly prefers cabbage-family plants like collards, mustard, and kale, especially in the South.
seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica) is a brassica-specialist stink bug, most damaging in the southern United States, where it completes two to four generations a year and overwinters as an adult in debris and weeds.

beginner: Search out and crush the bugs, their eggs (little barrel-shaped eggs in rows), and young ones by hand. Use a row cover to keep them off, pull out badly infested plants, and clear away weeds and old plants where they hide over winter.
seasoned: Hand-pick and crush adults, nymphs, and the barrel-shaped egg rows; exclude with floating row cover; remove heavily infested plants. Pyrethrins are permitted in organic production if pressure is severe.

beginner: Clean up garden debris and cabbage-family weeds where the adults overwinter, use row cover, and consider a trap crop of mustard or an early collard planting to lure them away from the main crop, then destroy it.
seasoned: Eliminate overwintering sites by removing crop debris and crucifer weeds, use row cover, and deploy an early trap crop of mustard, collards, or rapeseed to divert overwintering adults, then destroy it before the main crop is set out.

beginner: You'll see clusters of tiny soft insects on the new growth and tucked into the leaf folds, often a waxy gray-green kind. Leaves curl and pucker, and there may be a sticky coating.
seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on growing tips and leaf undersides; the waxy gray-green cabbage aphid is especially troublesome because it lodges in the crown and leaf folds and is hard to wash out at harvest.

beginner: Aphids are tiny insects that suck juice from the plant. They breed fast and hide deep in the leaf folds and growing tip, where they are hard to wash out.
seasoned: Several aphid species, notably the cabbage aphid, suck sap from collards; they multiply quickly and their feeding distorts growth and contaminates the harvested leaves. Populations explode in warm weather, so summer collards need close scouting.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap or neem oil, making sure to hit under the leaves and into the folds where they hide. Repeat every few days.
seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water, or spray insecticidal soap or neem, covering leaf undersides and the crown; repeat every few days. Catch infestations early before they lodge in the growing point.

beginner: Welcome helpful bugs like ladybugs and lacewings that eat aphids, don't overdo the nitrogen fertilizer (lush growth attracts them), and check the new growth often.
seasoned: Encourage natural enemies like ladybugs and lacewings, avoid overfeeding nitrogen (which spurs the soft growth aphids favor), and inspect growing tips early so colonies do not lodge in the crown.

beginner: Lots of tiny round holes in the leaves of young plants, made by small dark beetles that jump away like fleas when you get close. Bad damage can stunt seedlings.
seasoned: Tiny round shot-hole pits chewed in the leaves of young plants; the small dark beetles jump like fleas when disturbed. Heavy feeding stunts or kills seedlings and scars the leaves of a leaf crop.

beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew on young cabbage-family leaves. They hurt seedlings most, because a tiny plant can't grow fast enough to recover.
seasoned: Flea beetles chew the foliage of young brassicas and are most damaging at the seedling stage; on collards they also leave cosmetic shot-holes in the harvested leaves.

beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover, and if there are a lot of beetles, use a spray such as spinosad or a kaolin clay coating. The main goal is to get the seedlings big enough to handle it.
seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover, and spray spinosad or apply kaolin clay if pressure is high; the goal is getting plants past the vulnerable seedling stage.

beginner: Cover seedlings with row cover from the start, keep them strong with steady water and food so they grow past the damage, and pull nearby weeds in the cabbage family.
seasoned: Use row cover from sowing or transplanting, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and feeding so they grow through the damage, and clean up weedy brassica relatives nearby.

beginner: New transplants wilt and grow badly or fall over. If you pull one up, you'll find small white maggots eating the roots. It's worst in cool, wet spring soil.
seasoned: Transplants wilt, grow poorly, and may collapse; pulling a plant reveals small white maggots tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Damage is worst in cool, wet spring soil, so it bites the early spring planting more than the fall one.

beginner: A small fly lays eggs at the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow down and eat the roots. The fly is most active in cool spring weather.
seasoned: The larvae of the cabbage root fly tunnel into brassica roots; the adult lays eggs at the stem base, and the maggots feed on the roots below, sometimes killing young plants.

beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots you can't save that plant, so pull and throw away the badly damaged ones. Put your effort into protecting the rest from new eggs.
seasoned: There is no effective rescue once maggots are in the roots; remove and destroy badly affected plants and protect the rest from further egg-laying.

beginner: Put a small collar or disk around the base of each transplant to stop the fly from laying eggs there, or use a row cover. Don't plant into cold, soggy soil, and avoid spots where you grew cabbage-family plants last year.
seasoned: Place a collar or disk around the stem base at transplanting to block egg-laying, or use row cover; avoid planting into cold, wet soil and rotate away from where brassicas grew.

beginner: Plants wilt in the afternoon, stay small and yellowish, and don't bounce back. If you dig one up, the roots are swollen into lumpy, club-shaped knobs.
seasoned: Plants wilt in the heat of the day, grow stunted and yellowed, and recover poorly; roots are swollen into distorted clubs and galls instead of normal fine roots.

beginner: A germ that lives in the soil infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and makes them swell, which stops the plant from taking up water and food. It stays in the soil for years.
seasoned: A soilborne organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) infects brassica roots and causes the galls, which block water and nutrient uptake. It persists in soil for many years and spreads in contaminated soil and water.

beginner: There's no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. Adding lime to make the soil less acidic (closer to neutral) helps hold it back, and growing cabbage-family plants only rarely in that spot starves the germ out.
seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Raising soil pH toward 7.0 or above with lime can suppress the disease, and long rotations starve it out over time.

beginner: Don't grow collards or their cabbage-family relatives in the same spot more than once every 3 years, or longer if you've had clubroot. Keep the soil from being too acidic, improve drainage, and clean soil off your tools.
seasoned: Rotate brassicas on a cycle of at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is known; keep soil pH up, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil on tools and boots.

beginner: Yellow patches shaped like the letter V appear at the leaf edges, pointing inward, with black veins inside them. It can spread through the plant and rot the leaves you want to eat.
seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions spread inward from the leaf margins, with the veins inside the V turning black; the disease moves through the vascular system and can blacken and rot the harvested leaves. Warm, wet Southern weather drives it hard.

beginner: A bacteria that often comes in on infected seeds or transplants. It gets into the leaves and travels through the plant's veins, spreading fastest in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: A seedborne bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris) that enters through leaf pores and wounds and moves through the plant's veins; it spreads in warm, wet conditions and on infected seed or transplants.

beginner: There's no real cure, so remove and destroy infected plants to keep it from spreading. Don't handle or brush against the plants while they're wet, because that spreads the bacteria.
seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Avoid working among plants when foliage is wet, since that moves the bacteria.

beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, don't plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently, space plants for good airflow, and avoid overhead watering.
seasoned: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, rotate away from brassicas, give plants room for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and handling wet foliage.

beginner: Small dark spots on the leaves that grow into round patches with concentric rings, like a tiny target. Bad cases make the leaves yellow and unusable.
seasoned: Small dark lesions enlarge into circular spots with characteristic concentric rings (a target-spot look) and a yellow halo; because the leaves are the crop, even moderate spotting reduces the harvest. Favored by warm, wet conditions.

beginner: A fungus that spreads in warm, wet weather and infects the leaves, leaving target-like spots. It's worse on stressed plants and in crowded, damp plantings.
seasoned: Fungi in the genus Alternaria (with Cercospora causing a similar leaf spot) infect brassica foliage, spreading by spores in wind and splashing water; infected seed, crop debris, and long leaf wetness drive it.

beginner: Remove and destroy badly spotted leaves, improve airflow so leaves dry quickly, and use a copper spray if it spreads. Avoid wetting the leaves when you water.
seasoned: Remove and destroy spotted leaves and debris, improve airflow, avoid overhead watering, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high.

beginner: Start with clean seed, rotate away from brassicas, space plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and keep plants healthy so they resist infection.
seasoned: Use clean, disease-free seed, rotate away from brassicas, space for airflow, water at the soil line, and clear crop debris that harbors spores.

beginner: Pale yellow blotches on top of the leaves, with fuzzy grayish growth on the underside, mostly in cool, damp weather. Bad cases discolor the leaves.
seasoned: Pale yellow patches form on the upper leaf surface with a fuzzy gray-white growth underneath, mainly in cool, damp weather; severe infection discolors and downgrades the leaves.

beginner: A mold-like disease that loves cool, wet, humid weather and spreads through the air and water. Wet leaves and crowded plants make it worse.
seasoned: A fungus-like organism that thrives in cool, wet, humid conditions and spreads by spores in water and air; long leaf wetness and crowded plantings favor it. Collards' cool-season window overlaps the weather it likes.

beginner: Open up the airflow so leaves can dry, remove the worst leaves, and use a copper spray if it's spreading. It's hard to stop once the weather stays damp.
seasoned: Improve airflow and let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high; the disease is hard to stop once humidity stays high.

beginner: Space plants so air moves between them, water at the soil instead of from above, and pick resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
seasoned: Space plants for good air movement, water at the soil line rather than overhead, and choose resistant varieties where downy mildew is common.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week.
seasoned: Give about 1 to 1.5 inches weekly, kept even through the season, and more in hot, dry spells.

beginner: Aim for roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, more when it is hot.
seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week, leaning to the high end during summer heat in the South.

beginner: Water at the base of the plant rather than over the leaves.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose where possible.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant looks soggy and limp.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and limp, soft growth; collards dislike waterlogged soil and can rot at the crown.

beginner: Wilting leaves that turn tough and bitter, especially in hot weather.
seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, and tough, stringy, bitter leaves; drought stress is the main cause of poor leaf quality, especially in summer heat.

beginner: Keep the soil or tray damp while the seeds come up, without letting the surface dry out.
seasoned: Keep the seedbed or tray surface evenly moist through germination; brassica seed is shallow and should not dry mid-emergence.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly damp as they grow.
seasoned: Grow the seedlings on with steady, even moisture.

beginner: Water evenly as the plant grows its big leaves. Steady water keeps them tender and mild.
seasoned: Keep even moisture as the plant builds its leafy frame; steady water sets up tender, mild leaves.

beginner: Keep watering evenly while you pick leaves over the season, and give extra in summer heat. Drought makes collard leaves tough and strong-tasting.
seasoned: Steady moisture through the main leaf-production weeks, and especially through summer heat in warm regions, matters most for tender, mild leaves; drought makes them tough and strong. Pick lower leaves and keep watering to keep them coming.

beginner: In winter collards need little watering, and frost makes them sweeter. Do not keep cold soil soggy.
seasoned: In cold weather a hardy collard plant needs little supplemental water, and frost sweetens the leaves. Avoid waterlogging cold soil.

beginner: Keep the water steady so the leaves stay tender, not tough, and water more in hot weather.
seasoned: Even moisture is the key to tender, mild collard leaves; the crop holds through summer heat far better when it never dries out, since dry spells make the leaves tough and bitter.

beginner: Water steadily while the plant is making lots of leaves, and keep it up through summer heat.
seasoned: Steady moisture through the main leaf-production weeks, and especially during summer heat in warm regions, matters most for tender, mild leaves.

beginner: You can sow collard seeds right in the garden or start them indoors. For spring, start seeds about a month before planting out, and set plants in the garden a few weeks before your last frost, or just sow seeds once the soil can be worked. For a fall crop, sow in mid to late summer so it is ready before winter. Space full-size plants 18 to 24 inches apart. If you grow your own transplants, let them get used to the outdoors over a week before planting.
seasoned: Collards can be direct sown or transplanted, and in the South direct sowing is the norm. For a spring crop, start seeds indoors about 4 to 5 weeks before set-out and transplant around 3 to 4 weeks before the last frost, or direct sow as soon as the soil is workable; collards tolerate frost. For a fall and winter crop, sow in mid to late summer so plants size up before cold, then harvest through fall and, in mild zones, winter. Harden transplants off over 7 to 10 days. Thin or set plants 18 to 24 inches apart for full-size plants.

beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
seasoned: A light, well-drained commercial potting mix high in organic matter.

beginner: Mix in some compost for a steady supply of nutrients.
seasoned: Blend in compost and a slow-release nitrogen source; container collards still feed steadily.

beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather.
seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in heat and water before the mix dries out.

beginner: Feed a bit more often than in the ground, since watering washes nutrients out of pots.
seasoned: Container collards need more frequent feeding than in-ground plants because watering leaches nutrients.

beginner: In mild-winter areas, a potted collard keeps going through winter; just move it to a sheltered, sunny spot. In cold areas, pull the pot against the house or into an unheated garage during hard freezes, or grow a fast variety and enjoy it before deep winter.
seasoned: Collards are very cold-hardy and overwinter in a container in mild zones, where they keep producing through winter in a sheltered, sunny spot. In colder zones the limited root volume of a pot freezes harder than open ground, so move containers against a wall or into an unheated structure during hard freezes, or treat the potted crop as a single fall-into-winter planting.

beginner: Collards grow into big plants, so give each one a pot of at least 5 gallons that is 12 inches or more deep, one plant per pot. Keep it watered and fed, and pick the lower leaves as you need them. In hot areas, give it some afternoon shade.
seasoned: Collards make a good container crop, but they get large, so size up: use a container of at least 5 gallons and 12 inches deep, one plant per pot, and keep moisture even since pots dry quickly. Crop the lower leaves and leave the growing point, and in warm regions give afternoon shade and avoid heat-absorbing dark pots.

beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which keeps collard leaves tender.
seasoned: A self-watering container suits collards well, since it smooths out the steady moisture that keeps the leaves tender and mild.

beginner: Collards get tall and leafy, so give each one a roomy pot that holds at least 5 gallons and is about 12 inches deep. A wide, heavy pot is better than a tall skinny one because it holds moisture and keeps the big plant from tipping over.
seasoned: Collards build a tall stem and a heavy rosette of large leaves over a long season, so choose a container at least 5 gallons and 12 inches deep, one plant per pot. A broad, sturdy pot keeps the top-heavy plant from tipping and buffers the fast drying that narrow pots suffer.

beginner: Georgia is an easy, tough heirloom that takes heat and poor soil, great for beginners. Vates and Champion are compact and very cold-hardy, perfect for a fall or winter crop. Top Bunch and Blue Max are fast hybrids if you want tender leaves sooner. Morris Heading makes a softer, cabbage-like collard.
seasoned: Match the variety to the slot. Georgia (Georgia Southern) is the heat- and stress-tolerant Southern heirloom for summer-into-fall production; Vates and Champion are compact, bolt-resistant, very cold-hardy types that shine in fall and overwintering. Top Bunch and Blue Max are fast, uniform hybrids for quick, repeated cutting. Morris Heading is the traditional heading collard for a milder, more tender leaf. Where clubroot or other brassica diseases are a concern, look for resistant cultivars.

beginner: Other cabbage-family crops like broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, kale, and turnips.
seasoned: Other brassicas (broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, kale, Brussels sprouts, kohlrabi, turnip, radish, mustard), which share clubroot and cabbage-family pests.

beginner: Do not plant collards or other cabbage-family crops in the same spot year after year. Waiting at least 3 years between them, and longer if you have had clubroot, helps avoid soil diseases.
seasoned: Rotate so collards and their brassica relatives do not return to the same ground for at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is present, since the clubroot organism persists in soil for years. Keeping soil pH near neutral also helps suppress clubroot. In the South, where collards are grown nearly year-round, planning that rotation across beds takes extra thought.

beginner: Do not leave collards out on the counter. They wilt fast in the warmth, so get them into the fridge soon after picking.
seasoned: Collards wilt and toughen at room temperature and lose quality within a day or two, so do not leave them out. Refrigerate as soon as possible after cutting; if they must sit briefly, stand the stems in water like cut flowers.

beginner: Store collards unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge's crisper drawer, where they stay good for about a week, sometimes up to 2 weeks if very cold. Wait to wash them until you are ready to cook.
seasoned: Refrigerate unwashed in a loose or perforated bag in the crisper; collards hold their quality for roughly 1 week, and up to about 10 to 14 days held near 32°F at high humidity, a bit longer than tender greens because the leaves are sturdier. Washing before storage traps moisture and speeds spoilage.

beginner: Collards freeze well if you blanch them first. Strip the leaves off the tough stems, boil them for about 3 minutes, cool them right away in ice water, drain, and freeze.
seasoned: Collards freeze well once blanched: strip the leaves from the tough stems, blanch about 3 minutes in boiling water, cool quickly in ice water, drain, and freeze. Blanching halts the enzymes that otherwise cause off-flavors and loss of color in storage.

beginner: Collards are best right after you pick them, and the plant is its own best storage: in cool weather the leaves keep on the plant for weeks and even get sweeter after frost. So pick what you need when you need it, and chill it quickly after cutting.
seasoned: Quality is highest straight from the garden, and a key collard advantage is that the plant itself is the best storage: leaves keep on the plant for weeks in cool weather and sweeten after frost, so harvest close to when you will use them rather than stockpiling. Chilling promptly after cutting keeps the leaves crisp and mild.

beginner: In about 5 to 10 days, your seeds sprout and push up their first two little leaves (the seed leaves).
seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 5 to 10 days at soil temperatures of roughly 45 to 85°F, pushing up two seed leaves (cotyledons).

beginner: Keep the soil damp. Once the first real collard leaves appear after the seed leaves, thin crowded seedlings.
seasoned: Keep the seedbed or starting mix evenly moist; thin or pot up once the first true leaves appear.

beginner: Have your seeds come up yet?
seasoned: Did your collard seeds sprout?

beginner: The seedlings grow their real, smooth leaves and a stronger stem. They are ready to move outside at about 4 to 5 weeks old.
seasoned: Young plants develop true leaves and a sturdy stem; collard transplants are ready at about 4 to 5 weeks. Flea beetles are the main seedling threat.

beginner: If you grew transplants, harden them off over about a week before planting out. Watch for flea beetle shot-holes on the young leaves.
seasoned: Harden off over 7 to 10 days before setting out; thin or set plants 18 to 24 inches apart and protect seedlings from flea beetles with row cover.

beginner: How many real leaves do your seedlings have?
seasoned: How many true leaves does your seedling have?

beginner: The plant grows into a tall stem with a bunch of big leaves on top. This is when it builds the frame that you will harvest from for months.
seasoned: The plant builds an upright stem topped with a rosette of large leaves over several weeks, laying down the productive frame.

beginner: Feed with nitrogen and keep it evenly watered so the leaves stay tender. Check for aphids in the growing tip and caterpillars and harlequin bugs on the leaves.
seasoned: Side-dress with nitrogen, keep moisture even for tender leaves, and scout for aphids, cabbageworms, and harlequin bugs while the frame fills out.

beginner: Is your plant growing lots of healthy leaves?
seasoned: Are your collards putting on healthy leafy growth?

beginner: Once the lower leaves are about 8 to 10 inches, start picking. Take the lowest, outside leaves and leave the center to keep growing, so the plant gives leaves for months. Or cut the whole young plant.
seasoned: Lower leaves reach usable size (8 to 10 inches) at about 55 to 75 days; harvest cut-and-come-again, taking the lowest leaves and leaving the growing bud, or cut whole young plants at 6 to 10 inches.

beginner: Pick the outer leaves regularly, never stripping more than about a third at once. Feed lightly after a big harvest. The leaves taste sweeter after frost.
seasoned: Crop the outer leaves regularly to keep new growth coming, side-dress lightly after heavy picking, and expect the best flavor after a frost.

beginner: Have you started picking outer leaves?
seasoned: Are you harvesting outer leaves?

beginner: Feed with nitrogen and water steadily, about 1 to 1.5 inches a week, so the leaves stay tender and mild.
seasoned: Side-dress nitrogen as the plant builds and keep moisture even at roughly 1 to 1.5 inches per week; drought stress is the top cause of tough, stringy leaves, especially in heat.

seasoned: Scout the growing tip and crown for cabbage aphids, the leaves for cabbageworms, and, in the South, for harlequin bugs; catching them early keeps the harvested leaves clean.

beginner: Pick the lowest leaves when they are about hand-sized or bigger, and leave the center growing, so the same plant keeps making leaves. Or cut the whole young plant and let it grow back.

New growers often pick too timidly or take the bud, which stalls the plant.

beginner: Your collards shot up a tall stalk with buds or yellow flowers and the leaves turned bitter. Collards are biennials that bolt (run to flower) mostly in their second spring after a cold winter, and sometimes from heat and long days on a stressed plant. Once they bolt the leaves go bitter and tough. People often blame the plant, but it is just its life cycle. Next time crop overwintered plants out before the stalk elongates, choose bolt-resistant cultivars (Vates, Champion, Top Bunch), and avoid drought stress.

beginner: Your collards stayed small and yellowish, wilted in the afternoon, and when you dug them up the roots were swollen into lumps. That is clubroot, a soil disease that infects cabbage-family roots and lasts for years in the soil. It usually builds up when brassicas are grown in the same spot repeatedly, which is easy to do with a near-year-round crop. Next time, rotate so cabbage-family crops do not return to that bed for at least 3 years, keep the soil pH near neutral, and improve drainage.
seasoned: Plants were stunted and chlorotic, wilted by day, and showed galled, clubbed roots, the signature of clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae). The soilborne organism persists for years and builds under repeated brassica cropping and acidic, poorly drained soil, a real risk where collards are grown nearly year-round. Next time rotate cabbage-family crops out for at least 3 years (longer where known), lime toward a neutral-to-slightly-alkaline pH, and improve drainage; there is no in-season cure.

beginner: Rotate brassicas out of that bed for at least 3 years, keep soil pH near neutral, and improve drainage.
seasoned: Use a 3-year-plus brassica rotation, raise pH toward neutral, and improve drainage; remove and destroy infected plants.

beginner: Plant collards in small batches a couple of weeks apart, in spring and again in late summer for fall, rather than all at once. Each plant keeps giving leaves for a long time, so you do not need many. In hot-desert and tropical areas, skip the peak summer and plant for fall and winter.
seasoned: Collards crop over a long window, so rather than one big planting, sow small batches every 2 to 3 weeks through the cool stretches of spring and again from late summer for a fall and winter crop. Because each plant is cropped over many weeks, you need fewer sowings than for a fast crop, but staggering keeps tender young leaves coming. In the South you can plant across most of the year; only in genuinely extreme heat (deserts, peak Florida and Hawaii summers) do you skip the peak and plant for fall and winter instead.

Collards are the hardiest cole crop, so harvest stretches later than most greens; under a low tunnel it can reach into winter, but deep cold eventually ends the open-ground crop.

beginner: Collards are a leafy cousin of kale and cabbage, grown for their big, smooth green leaves. They are the famous green of Southern cooking, and they are tough: they handle cold better than almost any other vegetable and get sweeter after frost, but they also keep growing in summer heat that stops other greens. The plant grows tall with a bunch of large leaves at the top. You pick the lower leaves a few at a time for months, or cut the whole young plant. In warm areas collards grow almost all year; in cooler areas they do best in spring and fall.
seasoned: Collards (Brassica oleracea, Acephala group) are a loose-leaf, non-heading cabbage relative grown for their large, smooth blue-green leaves, the same species as kale and the classic green of Southern gardens. Their signature is unusual tolerance of BOTH cold and heat: collards are the most cold-hardy of the cole crops, sweetening after frost and holding through hard freezes, yet they are also the most heat-tolerant, producing right through Southern summers where lettuce and most brassicas have long since bolted. A collard plant builds a stout upright stem topped with a rosette of broad leaves, and you crop the lower leaves over a long run or cut the whole young plant. In much of the South they grow nearly year-round; everywhere else they shine in the long cool shoulders of spring and fall.

beginner: Begin picking when the lower leaves are about the size of your hand or bigger, around 8 to 10 inches. Take the lowest, outside leaves and leave the middle growing, so the plant keeps making more for months. You can also cut the whole young plant off near the ground and let it grow back. The leaves taste best picked while still tender, and they get sweeter after a frost.
seasoned: Start cropping outer leaves once they reach about 8 to 10 inches, taking the lowest, oldest leaves first and leaving the central bud and upper rosette to keep producing. Leaves are most tender picked young to medium-sized; old leaves turn tough and stringy. Alternatively cut the whole young plant near the soil line at 6 to 10 inches and let it regrow, or harvest the tender inner rosette. Flavor is mildest and sweetest in cool weather and after a frost.

beginner: Collards like rich, loose soil with lots of compost mixed in. Dig the bed over and work in compost or aged manure before planting, since collards are hungry plants that grow a lot of leaves. Aim for a soil pH around 6.0 to 6.8, and make sure water drains away well. Keep the soil moist but not soggy and the plants will reward you with big, tender leaves.
seasoned: Collards are leafy heavy feeders that reward a fertile, well-drained loam worked deeply and enriched with compost or aged manure before planting. Loosen the bed 8 to 12 inches, mix in organic matter for steady moisture and nitrogen, and aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 6.8. Where clubroot has appeared, lime toward the high end of that band. Good drainage matters as much as fertility: collards make their best leaves in soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged.
